item.base_system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Mn20) with initial average grain size of 25 μm
item.intervention: Applied tensile creep stress of 140–200 MPa at 500–600 °C (Low-Stress Region)
item.processing: Tensile creep tests on flat dog-boned specimens (25 mm gauge length) using CSS-3905 machine; temperature measured with ±1 °C accuracy; strain measured by LVDT extensometer

records.text: Intervention effect. Base system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Mn20) with initial average grain size of 25 μm. Intervention: Applied tensile creep stress of 140–200 MPa at 500–600 °C (Low-Stress Region). Processing: Tensile creep tests on flat dog-boned specimens (25 mm gauge length) using CSS-3905 machine; temperature measured with ±1 °C accuracy; strain measured by LVDT extensometer. Test conditions: 500, 550, and 600 °C; stresses 140–200 MPa. Structure change: Obvious grain coarsening observed; dislocation densities low with few short straight segments and lath-shaped areas; no dynamic recrystallization or precipitation. Property change: Stress exponent n = 5 to 6; activation energy Q = 268 kJ mol−1. Mechanism: Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion. Evidence: measured. Quote: "In the low-stress region (subsequently denoted as LSR-region I), the stress exponent values vary in the range of 5 to 6, and the average activation energy Q takes a value of 268 kJ mol −1."

item.intervention: Applied tensile creep stress of 320–400 MPa at 500–600 °C (High-Stress Region)
item.processing: Tensile creep tests on flat dog-boned specimens; interrupted at steady-state stages and cooled quickly under load using liquid nitrogen
item.structure_change: Complete dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement (average grain sizes 22–31 μm); high density of tangled and curved dislocations; formation of nano-sized precipitates (M23C6 or Cr-rich σ phase) at grain boundaries
item.property_change: Stress exponent n = 8.9–14; activation energy Q = 380 kJ mol−1 (average)
item.attributed_mechanism: Coordinative contributions of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation; precipitates act as barriers increasing activation energy
quotes: In the high-stress region (subsequently denoted as HSR-region II), the stress exponents are in the range of 8.9–14, and the activation energy is Q = 359–410 kJ/mol with an average value of 380 kJ mol −1.
Higher stress levels (500 °C/400MPa and 600 °C/320MPa) lead to the formation of completely recrystallized and refined microstructures
Considerable precipitates of irregular shape were predominantly observed at the grain boundaries in HSR. The sizes of these precipitates were within a range of 50–200 nm

item.intervention: Increased testing temperature from 500 °C to 600 °C at constant stress (e.g., 200 MPa)
item.processing: Tensile creep tests with temperature measured by three thermocouples; strain continuously measured by LVDT
item.structure_change: Transition from few short straight dislocation segments to extensively curved or looped dislocations; increased dislocation activity
item.property_change: Creep rate increases; stress exponent remains in LSR range (5–6) but activation energy analysis shows temperature dependence
item.attributed_mechanism: Dislocation climb mechanism operative; temperature increases dislocation curvature and looping
quotes: The substructures reveal increasing dislocation activity in LSR with increasing temperature, as the dislocations are extensively curved or even looped
The applied stress at which the transition occurred increased from 200 to 350 MPa, with the temperature decreasing from 600 to 500 °C.

item.base_system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy in HSR
item.intervention: Dynamic precipitation of M23C6 carbides and Cr-rich σ phase during creep
item.processing: Long-term deformation at elevated temperatures (500–600 °C) under high stress; interrupted for TEM analysis
item.structure_change: Formation of irregular precipitates (50–200 nm) at grain boundaries; identified as fcc M23C6 carbide or Cr-rich tetragonal σ phase
item.property_change: Contribution to abnormally high stress exponents (8.9–14) and increased activation energy (380 kJ mol−1)
item.attributed_mechanism: Precipitates exert boundary obstacle stress preventing dislocation annihilation; act as barriers for dislocation motion
quotes: Quantitative micro-EDS analysis indicates that the chemical compositions (at. %) of the precipitates take almost identical values of Cr = 26.6, Mn = 20.2, Fe = 18.9, Co = 17.5, Ni =16.6
The crystal structure of these precipitates is identified as fcc M 23 C 6 carbide with a lattice parameter of 1.06 nm
The precipitates act as barriers for dislocation motion via producing boundary obstacle stress, resulting in high activation energy for creep deformation.

records.text: Intervention effect. Base system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy. Intervention: Dynamic recrystallization during high-stress creep deformation. item.intervention: Application of stress levels causing transition from LSR to HSR
item.processing: Tensile creep tests with at least seven applied stress levels chosen for each temperature
item.test_conditions: Stress transition from 200 MPa to 350 MPa (at 600 °C) or 200 MPa to 350 MPa (at 500 °C)
item.structure_change: Transition from grain coarsening and low dislocation density to dynamic recrystallization and high dislocation density with precipitates
item.property_change: Stress exponent increases from 5–6 to 8.9–14; activation energy increases from 268 kJ mol−1 to 380 kJ mol−1
item.attributed_mechanism: Combined effects of dynamic recrystallization and precipitation cause abnormally high stress exponents and activation energy
quotes: The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II).
The applied stress at which the transition occurred increased from 200 to 350 MPa, with the temperature decreasing from 600 to 500 °C.
The abnormally high stress exponents in HSR were ascribed to the coordinative contributions of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation.

item.intervention: Dislocation jog and tangling configurations formation
item.processing: Creep deformation at 550 °C and 600 °C; TEM observation of dislocation substructures
item.structure_change: Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations frequently observed; cusped configurations with bowed segments; high density of tangled and curved dislocations
item.property_change: Indicates stress-assisted dislocation climb mechanism; contributes to high activation energy in HSR
item.attributed_mechanism: Jog configurations indicative of dislocation climb; dislocation tangling increases barriers for motion
quotes: Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively.
Such cusped configurations may be attributed to intrinsic pinning due to the occurrence of jogs along the screw dislocations
The tangled dislocations at 600 °C/320 MPa are severely curved, with a large number of loops formed in a wide range of sizes

item.intervention: Fracture under high stress in HSR
item.processing: Tensile creep tests to fracture; SEM examination of fracture surfaces
item.structure_change: Ductile rupture with dimples; slip striations notable at 600 °C; Mn-containing oxides visible on fracture surfaces
item.property_change: Ductile transgranular fracture despite high stress; contrary to common brittle failure expectations
item.attributed_mechanism: Ductile creep failure associated with dislocation interactions generating vacancies and void nucleation
quotes: All the fractographs in Figure 10 for HSR from 500 °C to 600 °C exhibit typical ductile rupture, where both the width and depth of dimples increase with temperature.
It is worth noting that the crept samples fracture in a ductile transgranular manner at high stress, which is contrary to common knowledge
The ductile creep failure may be associated with the dislocation interactions during high-temperature deformation, which contribute to the progressive generation of vacancies and nucleation of voids.

item.intervention: Normalization of creep data using diffusion-compensated strain rate and modulus-compensated stress
item.processing: Data analysis plotting ε˙kTexp(Q/RT)/G versus σ/G with G = 85 − 16/(e448/T − 1)
item.test_conditions: All tested temperatures (500–600 °C) and stress levels
item.structure_change: Data points in both stress regions represented by single lines with slopes 5.5 (LSR) and 10.6 (HSR)
item.property_change: Confirms lattice diffusion control in both regions despite high stress exponents in HSR
item.attributed_mechanism: Creep deformation in both stress regions dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion
quotes: The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
It is evident that almost all data points in the two stress regions at different temperatures can be represented by a single line with a respective slope of 5.5 and 10.6 for LSR and HSR.
This strongly implies that creep deformation in both regions may be controlled by lattice diffusion of constituent elements in the alloy.

item.intervention: Severe initial deformation and plastic flow to establish constant stress state
item.processing: Creep tests where samples experience drastic plastic deformation in short time
item.structure_change: Some grains severely elongated; extra barriers for dynamic recovery and recrystallization
item.property_change: Contributes to increased activation energy for creep deformation
item.attributed_mechanism: Severe initial deformation exerts extra influence on increasing barriers for dynamic recovery and recrystallization
quotes: The samples experience drastic plastic deformation in a short time to establish a constant stress state for subsequent creep deformation.
As a result, some grains are severely elongated, which, in turn, exerts an extra influence on increasing the barriers for dynamic recovery and recrystallization.
Simultaneously, the barriers imposed by these precipitates and severe initial deformation were referred to so as to increase the activation energy for creep deformation.

item.processing: Calculation and comparison of Q = 268 kJ mol−1 with literature values (288–317 kJ mol−1)

item.property_change: Activation energy comparable to lattice diffusion of constituent elements

Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion is suggested as a possible rate-dominating mechanism at low stresses.

item.intervention: Identification of precipitate phases via SAED and EDS
item.processing: TEM observations with selected area electron diffraction and micro-EDS analysis
item.structure_change: Identification of fcc M23C6 carbide (lattice parameter 1.06 nm) and Cr-rich tetragonal σ phase (lattice parameters a/c = 0.916/0.509 nm)
item.property_change: Precipitates contribute to high stress exponents and activation energy via boundary obstacle stress
item.attributed_mechanism: Precipitates prevent annihilation of moving dislocations at boundaries; act as barriers

The precipitates in the 50 °C/360MPa crept alloy are concluded to be Cr-rich tetragonal σ phase with lattice parameters of a/c = 0.916/0.509 nm.
The stress controlling the dislocation velocity is reduced to an effective value obtained by subtracting the stress necessary for overcoming precipitates from the applied stress.
